newsitem.title: UK: Five hurt in Belfast attack on security forces.
newsitem.headline: Five hurt in Belfast attack on security forces.

text.p: Five members of the security forces were injured in Northern Ireland on Friday when a joint police and British army patrol came under a gun and bomb attack in a republican area of Belfast, security sources said.
Ambulances were rushed to the scene after two police officers and three soldiers were hit in the late evening attack.
A police spokesman said: "We have got five casualties, both Royal Ulster Constabulary and military. It happened in a terrorist attack."

One resident said he heard about 20 shots fired at the patrol after gunmen believed to be republican guerrillas got out of a car to attack the patrol as it carried out a vehicle check in the city's Ardoyne area, a Catholic nationalist stronghold.
"They came under gun and bomb attack," a police official said.
Security forces have come under sniper attack in the past week during violence triggered by a Protestant march along the Catholic Garvaghy road area of Portadown, south of Belfast.
Hospital sources said that one of the casualties was a woman aged 30, who was wounded in the thigh and arm. She was said to be in stable condition.
The sources said other casualties were taken to Musgrave Park, a military hospital in Belfast.
Police said none of the casualties suffered life-threatening injuries.
After the attack, armoured troop carriers moved into the area which was sealed off by police.

Local media reported that earlier in the evening, leaflets purporting to come from a previously unheard-of group called the Cliftonville-Oldpark Defence Committee had been pushed through people's doors, telling them to stay off the streets.
The incident came after it appeared that tension had subsided when the Protestant Orange Order announced it was cancelling four flashpoint parades in Belfast and other towns.
Cecil Walker, the local member of parliament for the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, said the shooting was a bitter disappointment after the Orange decision to cancel its contentious parades.
"We were hoping things were going to be better than they were," he said. "But there are obviously elements in the nationalist community who seem to be holding on to mayhem," he said.
